Price, size, and condition for 21,000 houses

The pipeline

Nothing in this chapter is new. It is every earlier chapter, in order, on one dataset.

Import, Wrangle, Visualize, Model

  • Import the data and look at what you actually have.
  • Wrangle it into the shape the question needs.
  • Visualize before you model, always.
  • Model last, then say what it means in plain words.

Look first

Three things worth catching before you fit anything.

Data Quality

  • Skew: a long right tail makes a mean misleading.
  • Missing values: know how many, and why they are missing.
  • Outliers: decide whether they are errors or real cases.
  • A histogram of every numerical variable takes a minute and saves an hour.

log10()

A log transform pulls in a long right tail, turning a lopsided cloud into one a straight line can describe.

Tame The Skew

Price and size are both heavily right-skewed. Their logarithms are not.

mutate()

Create the transformed variables once, then model with them.

Example

house_prices <- house_prices |>
  mutate(log10_price = log10(price), log10_size = log10(sqft_living))

the verb (function) what to call the new column what to put in it

ggplot()

Plot the relationship, split by the categorical variable, before deciding what model to fit.

Example

one color per condition

ggplot(house_prices, aes(x = log10_size, y = log10_price, color = condition)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

one straight line per condition

make 21,000 points faint

interaction

If the clouds for different conditions trend at different angles, one shared slope will not do.

One Slope Per Group

An interaction gives each condition its own intercept and its own slope.

lm()

Use a star, not a plus: * fits an interaction, so each condition gets its own slope.

Example

the verb (function) interaction, not parallel slopes

price_interaction <- lm(log10_price ~ log10_size * condition,
                        data = house_prices)

the data frame

get_regression_table()

Read the coefficients, remembering that they are on the log10 scale, not in dollars.

Example

get_regression_table(price_interaction)
# A tibble: 10 × 7

Telling it

The last step is the one that gets graded in the real world.

Say What It Means

  • Translate coefficients back out of log scale before quoting them.
  • Name the units. A slope without units is not a finding.
  • Say what the model cannot tell you, including anything causal.
  • One clear plot beats a table of numbers for a non-technical reader.
